blocks.text: Welcome to the Neuroscience Lab

Neuroscience studies the nervous system — how neurons signal, how circuits compute, how the brain gives rise to mind and behavior. Four modes guide your research: Principles (established knowledge), Projects (dissections, models, recordings), Hypotheses (open questions about consciousness and computation), and News (latest papers and discoveries).
Pick a branch below. Each branch has levels. Read Principles, try a Project, ponder a Hypothesis, and check News. Depth tabs (Understand → Explore → Go Deeper → Research) reveal more detail.
Physics was the first lab. Neuroscience is second. More labs open later.

children.title: Cellular & Molecular Neuroscience
children.description: Neurons, glia, ion channels, synapses, neurotransmitters, signaling.

blocks.text: The Neuron — Structure & Function

A neuron has four main parts: dendrites (receive signals), cell body/soma (integrates), axon (conducts action potential), and axon terminals (release neurotransmitters). Myelin sheaths (from oligodendrocytes/Schwann cells) speed conduction via saltatory propagation at Nodes of Ranvier.
Dendrites: input. Soma: integration + nucleus. Axon: output cable. Axon hillock: spike initiation zone. Terminals: synaptic output.
Build a neuron model: Use pipe cleaners (dendrites), foam ball (soma), string (axon), beads (terminals). Label each part and trace signal direction (dendrite → soma → axon → terminal).
Why do neurons have branching dendrites but a single axon? Hypothesis: Dendrites collect thousands of inputs; one axon ensures a single, consistent output to downstream cells.
The Action Potential

Neurons signal with electrical spikes — action potentials. At rest, the membrane is polarized (~−70 mV). Depolarization to threshold (~−55 mV) opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → rapid depolarization (~+30 mV) → K⁺ channels open → repolarization → hyperpolarization → refractory period. All-or-none: once threshold is reached, the spike fires fully.
Resting → Threshold → Depolarization (Na⁺ in) → Repolarization (K⁺ out) → Hyperpolarization → Refractory period.
An action potential either fires fully or not at all — there are no partial spikes. Stronger stimuli increase firing rate, not spike size.

Cockroach leg / worm preparation: Record extracellular spikes from an invertebrate nerve cord using a DIY amplifier (SpikerBox-style). Touch a sensory hair → observe spikes on a phone oscilloscope app.
Why the refractory period? Hypothesis: It prevents backward propagation of the spike and limits maximum firing frequency (~1 kHz).
Synapses & Neurotransmitters

Synapses are junctions where neurons communicate. Electrical synapses (gap junctions) are fast and bidirectional. Chemical synapses: presynaptic terminal releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell. Major neurotransmitters: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, norepinephrine.
Glutamate → depolarizes (EPSP). GABA/glycine → hyperpolarizes (IPSP). Summation of EPSPs/IPSPs at the axon hillock decides whether the postsynaptic cell spikes.
Neurotransmitter card sort: Sort neurotransmitters into excitatory/inhibitory/modulatory, and match each to a function (dopamine: reward/movement; serotonin: mood/sleep; ACh: muscle/memory).
How do antidepressants work if serotonin changes in hours but mood improves in weeks? Hypothesis: Downstream receptor adaptation and neuroplasticity, not just transmitter levels.

children.title: Circuits & Systems Neuroscience
children.description: Neural circuits, sensory systems, motor control, brain regions, networks.

blocks.text: Vision — From Photons to Perception

Light hits the retina: photoreceptors (rods: dim light; cones: color) → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve → LGN (thalamus) → primary visual cortex (V1). Retinal processing already computes contrast, edges, and motion before signals reach the brain. V1 detects orientation and spatial frequency; higher areas process faces, objects, motion.
The region of sensory space that, when stimulated, drives a neuron. V1 simple cells have oriented, elongated receptive fields (edge detectors).

Afterimage demo: Stare at a colored square for 30 seconds, then look at a white wall. You see the complementary color — opponent-process cells in retina/LGN are fatigued, revealing the opponent channel.
How does V1 bind color, orientation, and motion into one object? Hypothesis: Feature integration via synchronized neural oscillations (gamma band, ~40 Hz). The binding problem remains debated.
Motor Control

Motor hierarchy: spinal reflexes (fastest, local) → brainstem (posture, locomotion) → motor cortex + cerebellum + basal ganglia (voluntary movement, coordination, learning). Upper motor neurons (cortex) → lower motor neurons (spinal cord → muscle). The stretch reflex (knee jerk) is the simplest circuit: sensory → spinal interneuron → motor neuron → muscle.
One lower motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates. Small units for fine control (eye, fingers); large units for power (quadriceps).
Knee-jerk reflex: Tap the patellar tendon; observe leg kick. It's monosynaptic (sensory → motor neuron in spinal cord) — no brain needed. Compare reaction time to a voluntary button press.
Why do we have both cerebellum and basal ganglia for movement? Hypothesis: Cerebellum = timing, coordination, error correction; basal ganglia = action selection, gating, habit learning.

children.title: Cognition & Behavior
children.description: Memory, learning, attention, language, emotion, decision-making.

blocks.text: Memory & Learning

Memory systems: sensory (milliseconds), short-term/working (seconds, ~7 items), long-term (years). Long-term splits into declarative (facts/events, hippocampal-dependent) and procedural (skills, habits, striatal). Learning = synaptic plasticity: long-term potentiation (LTP, strengthening) and long-term depression (LTD, weakening). Hebb's rule: 'cells that fire together, wire together.'
When neuron A repeatedly helps fire neuron B, the synapse A→B strengthens. Cellular basis of associative learning.

Human memory span test: Read digit strings of increasing length to a friend; find their forward digit span (typically 5–9). Test recall after distraction — working memory fades fast without rehearsal.
Where is a specific memory stored? Hypothesis: Engram — distributed across cell assemblies, with hippocampus as index for declarative memories (systems consolidation to cortex over time).
Emotion & Reward

Key structures: amygdala (threat, fear conditioning), nucleus accumbens + ventral tegmental area (reward, dopamine), prefrontal cortex (regulation, top-down control), insula (interoception, gut feelings). Dopamine signals reward prediction error — not pleasure itself, but 'better than expected' learning signals.
Dopamine bursts when reward exceeds prediction; dips when expected reward is omitted. This drives learning (Rescorla-Wagner model).
Pavlovian conditioning (human): Pair a neutral tone with a puff of air to the eye. After pairings, tone alone triggers blink. Measure trials to acquisition and extinction.
Is addiction a learning disorder? Hypothesis: Drugs hijack the dopamine prediction-error system, creating pathological learned associations between cues and reward.

children.title: Frontiers & Consciousness
children.description: Consciousness, brain-computer interfaces, neurodevelopment, disorders, AI-brain comparisons.

blocks.text: Consciousness — The Hard Problem

Consciousness has two aspects: easy problems (attention, integration, reportability, sleep/wake cycles — mechanistic) and the hard problem (why does processing feel like something? qualia). Leading theories: Global Workspace Theory (information broadcast to a 'theater'), Integrated Information Theory (consciousness = integrated information, Φ), Higher-Order Thought (awareness requires meta-representation). Neural correlates: posterior hot zone, prefrontal-parietal networks.
The minimal neural mechanisms sufficient for any specific conscious experience — e.g., V1 activity correlates with visual awareness, but isn't sufficient alone.
Binocular rivalry demo: Show different images to each eye (red/blue glasses). Perception flips spontaneously — consciousness selects one input despite constant sensory input. Record flip rate.

Could a digital computer be conscious? Hypothesis: Integrated Information Theory says maybe (if Φ is high); functionalists say yes (if it implements the right computations); biological naturalists say no (needs specific biology). Open question.
Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI)

BCIs read neural signals and translate them into commands. Non-invasive: EEG (scalp, millisecond timing, poor spatial resolution). Invasive: Utah arrays, Neuropixels (single-unit, high resolution, surgical risk). Applications: prosthetic control, communication for locked-in patients, sensory restoration (cochlear/retinal implants).
Electroencephalography — measures summed electrical activity of cortical neurons via scalp electrodes. Good temporal resolution (~ms), poor spatial resolution (~cm).
EEG alpha demo: Use an OpenBCI or Muse headset. Eyes closed → strong alpha (8–12 Hz) over occipital cortex; eyes open → alpha suppressed (visual input desynchronizes alpha).
Can BCI restore speech directly from thought? Hypothesis: Yes — recent studies decode attempted speech from motor cortex/sensorimotor signals at word-per-minute rates. Still early-stage.
